name: Mpoupieng
overview: A small forest group of the East, the Mpoupieng live mixed with the Baka, the Maka and the Djem, whose language they often speak. Their society, little hierarchical, grants prestige to the prosperous head of family; cash-crop and subsistence farming, palm wine and the balafon mark their life.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group, in close contact with the Baka, the Maka and the Djem; many speak Maka.
Neighbouring speech varieties exist at Batouri (mezime) and Yokadouma (pon-pon).
Marriages both within and outside the group; it is mostly women who marry outside.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Mpoupieng occupy their ancestral land, with no particular religious significance.
They come from the Yokadouma area, with a stopover at Etikeba, no ties kept.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Prestige goes to the married man, father of many children and owner of plantations.
The elders consult one another, then gather the population in an assembly to debate it.
Everybody can interact, but a distance is expected between children and adults, and between women and men.
Relations with neighbours are alliances.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband's family.
A boy becomes a man when he becomes a father and creates his plantation.
The reported ages at marriage are early.
Steps: presentation, bride price, marriage certificate.
Bride price: red wine (alliance, in memory of the blood shed at the girl's birth), fish, large basin, wrapper (compensation for the efforts made for her), blanket (gratitude towards her parents).

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship; sacred forests and mountains keep the memory of the group.
Birth welcomes a new person; death is the return to God.
Taboos: incest, food prohibitions for pregnant women and children; striking one's parents is a serious offence.
Divination by animal skins.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Cash-crop farming (commercial crops) and food-crop farming (tubers, cereals).
Each family inherits its plot.
Craftsmanship is not a tradition of the group.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Formerly, a bark loincloth (bila) for everyone.
Traditional medicine is considered effective and cheap.
Beauty: the strong, hard-working man, the full-figured woman.
Courtship: dance and gifts from the man; culinary talent and good manners from the woman.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Moambea rhythm, on the balafon; people dance at mourning ceremonies and weddings.
No community festival of its own.

sections.title: The names
items: The name is chosen by the heads of the family and does not change.
People are often called by a pseudonym (e.g. Messob); appellatives: miemo, motoum.
The founding ancestor is called Mpoh.

lessons.title: Who are the Mpoupieng? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Mpoupieng community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Mpoupieng community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Mpoupieng community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Mpoupieng community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Mpoupieng community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Mpoupieng call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Minority group, in close contact with the Baka, the Maka and the Djem; many speak Maka. • Neighbouring speech varieties exist in Batouri (mezime) and Yokadouma (pon-pon). • Marriages both within and outside the group; it is mainly women who marry outside. • The Mpoupieng occupy their ancestral land, with no particular religious significance. • They come from the Yokadouma area, with a stopover at Etikeba, with no links kept.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A small forest group of the East, the Mpoupieng live mixed with the Baka, the Maka and the Djem, whose language they often speak. Their society, little hierarchical, grants prestige to the prosperous head of family; cash-crop and subsistence farming, palm wine and the balafon mark their life.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Mpoupieng community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.instruction: On a timeline or a map, draw the migration route told in tradition.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Mpoupieng
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Mpoupieng organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Mpoupieng village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Mpoupieng organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Mpoupieng village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Prestige goes to the married man, father of many children and owner of plantations. • The elders consult together, then gather the population in an assembly to debate. • Everyone may interact, but distance is expected between children and adults, and between women and men. • Relations with neighbours are alliances.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Prestige goes to the married man, father of many children and owner of plantations. The elders consult one another and then gather the population in an assembly to debate it. Everyone may interact, but distance is expected between children and adults, and between women and men.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Mpoupieng, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.instruction: In groups: what are the advantages of making decisions by consensus?

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Mpoupieng
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Mpoupieng, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Mpoupieng.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Mpoupieng, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Mpoupieng.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: cassava leaves (kpwem) and tubers. • Drinks: palm wine, fermented banana. • Cash-crop farming (commercial crops) and food-crop farming (tubers, cereals). • Each family inherits its plot.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Mpoupieng eat mainly cassava leaves (kpwem) and tubers. Traditional drinks: palm wine, fermented banana. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Mpoupieng: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.instruction: Link each dish to the group's activities (agriculture, fishing, livestock rearing…).

activities.title: I present
activities.instruction: Prepare a poster for the class food fair.

student.memo: The Mpoupieng eat mainly cassava leaves (kpwem) and tubers. Traditional drinks: palm wine, fermented banana. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Clothing, adornments and crafts of the Mpoupieng
lessons.anelcac: Ways of life: clothing practices, crafts
objectives: Identify craft objects and their use
lessons.competence: Describe the clothing, adornments and craft objects of the Mpoupieng, and explain their use and value.
lessons.situation: A museum asks you to prepare a display case on the clothing and crafts of the Mpoupieng.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, craft objects or photos of craft objects, recycled materials.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How did people dress in the past, and how do they dress today? — Do clothes indicate status or occasion? — What objects are made, from what materials, and for what uses? — What are the criteria of beauty?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Mpoupieng
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Mpoupieng welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Mpoupieng family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Mpoupieng welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Mpoupieng family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The name is chosen by the heads of the family and does not change. • People are often called by a pseudonym (e.g. Messob); forms of address: miemo, motoum. • The founding ancestor is called Mpoh. • Birth welcomes a new person; death is the return to God. • A boy becomes a man when he becomes a father and creates his plantation.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The name is chosen by the heads of the family and does not change. People are often called by a pseudonym (e.g. Messob); terms of address: miemo, motoum. The founding ancestor is called Mpoh.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Explain the meaning of three Mpoupieng personal names and describe the moment when a child receives its name.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Marriage and bride price among the Mpoupieng
objectives: Putting the stages of marriage in order
Explain the symbolism of the bride price
lessons.competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Mpoupieng marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.
lessons.situation: Your elder brother wants to marry a young Mpoupieng woman. What steps will he have to follow?
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, props for the staging.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Mpoupieng marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Mpoupieng woman. Which steps will he have to follow?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband's family. • A boy becomes a man when he becomes a father and creates his plantation. • The reported ages at marriage are young. • Stages: introduction, bride price, marriage certificate. • Bride price: red wine (alliance, in memory of the blood shed at the girl's birth), fish, a large basin, a wrapper (compensation for the efforts made for her), a blanket (gratitude towards her parents).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Steps: presentation, bride price, marriage certificate. Bride price: red wine (alliance, in memory of the blood shed at the girl's birth), fish, large basin, wrapper (compensation for the efforts made for her), blanket (gratitude towards her parents).

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: In a group, act out a marriage proposal among the Mpoupieng, then explain the meaning of two elements of the bride price.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Mpoupieng
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Mpoupieng, choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Mpoupieng dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Mpoupieng, choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Mpoupieng dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.instruction: Among the Mpoupieng, traditional dances (mourning dances, wedding dances) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafon.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Mpoupieng
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mpoupieng, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Mpoupieng. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mpoupieng, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Mpoupieng. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No ancestor worship; sacred forests and mountains hold the group's memory. • Birth welcomes a new person; death is the return to God. • Taboos: incest, food prohibitions for pregnant women and children; hitting one's parents is a serious offence. • Divination with animal skins.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestor worship; sacred forests and mountains keep the memory of the group. Birth welcomes a new person; death is the return to God.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Mpoupieng (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Mpoupieng
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Mpoupieng and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Mpoupieng family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Mpoupieng greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Mpoupieng family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Mpoupieng. • Greetings: Oyiessée = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); We diémée = morning greeting (one person); Bi diémée = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Ngouot, Mbo, Lal, No, Tan. • The founding ancestor is called Mpoh.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Mpoupieng are the first steps towards communicating with the Mpoupieng. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Mpoupieng.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Mpoupieng are the first steps towards communicating with the Mpoupieng. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
